```{r, message=FALSE}
# call relevant libraries 
library(rpart)
library(randomForest)
library(randomForestExplainer)
library(ranger)
library(xgboost)
library(spdep)
library(spatialreg)
library(viridis)
library(data.table)
library(spectralGP)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(spgwr)
```

```{r}
# Set seed for the script 
set.seed(42)
```

```{r}
# Load in the data 
path <- "Data/train.csv"
df <- fread(path)
df
```
```{r}
# Initial data cleaning
colSums(is.na(df))
df[is.na(Age), Age := df[, median(Age, na.rm=T)]] 
df[, lapply(.SD, class)]
df[, Survived := as.factor(Survived)]
df[, Sex := as.factor(Sex)]
df[, Embarked := as.factor(Embarked)]
```



```{r}
# Question 1: Partition your data into an 80/20 train/test split. For all model fitting exercises, train/fit the model on the reserved 80% and validate on the reserved 20%
n <- nrow(df)
train_idx <- sample(seq_len(n), size = floor(0.80 * n))

train_data <- df[train_idx, , drop = FALSE]
test_data  <- df[-train_idx, , drop = FALSE]

nrow(train_data)
nrow(test_data)
```

```{r}
# Question 2: We’ll first fit a baseline model that isn’t “machine learning” (according to most people). Fit a multiple regression model that predicts titanic survivorship. Report the effects, their standard errors, and the overall accuracy of the model. Note: you must do logistic regression for this because the output is alive/dead or 1/0.

titanic_log <- glm(Survived ~ Pclass + Age + Fare, 
                   data = train_data, 
                   family = "binomial")
summary(titanic_log)

```

```{r}
# Predicted survival probability
probs <- predict(titanic_log, newdata = test_data, type = "response")
head(probs)

mean(probs, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r}
# Model p-value
with(titanic_log,
     pchisq(null.deviance - deviance,
            df.null - df.residual,
            lower.tail = FALSE))
```

```{r}
# Accuracy of the predictions on the test set
pred_class <- ifelse(probs > 0.5, 1, 0)

table(Predicted = pred_class, Actual = test_data$Survived)   
mean(pred_class == test_data$Survived, na.rm = TRUE)          

```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
# Question 3: Fit a RF model to describe survivorship 
train_data$Survived <- as.factor(train_data$Survived)
test_data$Survived  <- as.factor(test_data$Survived)

p        <- ncol(train_data) - 1          # number of predictors
mtry_set <- 1:min(5, p)              # mtry values to try
ntree    <- 1000

oob_mat <- matrix(NA, nrow = ntree, ncol = length(mtry_set),
                  dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("mtry=", mtry_set)))
rf_list <- list()

for (m in mtry_set) {
  rf <- randomForest(Survived ~ Pclass + Age + Fare, data = train_data,
                     ntree = ntree, mtry = m, importance = TRUE)
  rf_list[[as.character(m)]] <- rf
  oob_mat[, paste0("mtry=", m)] <- rf$err.rate[, "OOB"]
}
```

```{r}
# OOB error vs number of tree
matplot(1:ntree, oob_mat, type = "l", lty = 1, col = seq_along(mtry_set),
        xlab = "Number of trees", ylab = "OOB error rate",
        main = "OOB error vs. number of trees")
legend("topright", colnames(oob_mat), col = seq_along(mtry_set),
       lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

```{r}
# final OOB error vs mtry
final_oob <- oob_mat[ntree, ]
plot(mtry_set, final_oob, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "mtry (variables tried at each split)", ylab = "OOB error rate",
     main = "OOB error vs. mtry")
```



```{r}
# Choose the best model and report model accuracy
best_m  <- mtry_set[which.min(final_oob)]
best_rf <- rf_list[[as.character(best_m)]]
best_rf   
```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
# Variable Importance Plots 
plot_min_depth_distribution(best_rf)
plot_multi_way_importance(best_rf)
```

These plots show that the model works because it visualize how the model is influenced by the effects of a particular variable. We also see a clear negative correlation between the number of times that a variable is used to split the root node (times_a_root) and the average depth of the node closest to the root of the tree (mean_min_depth). The lower mean_min_root values indicate that a variable is more important as this variable can be used to split large portions of the dataset early on in the tree. It makes sense that the more influential variables are used by the model more often and thus are more effective as splitting the data. The trend between these factors suggests that the model is working as expected.

```{r}
# Compare OOB error with the error on the test data
pred     <- predict(best_rf, test_data)
test_acc <- mean(pred == test_data$Survived)
oob_acc  <- 1 - tail(best_rf$err.rate[, "OOB"], 1)
```

```{r}
# Make the confusion matrix 
table(Predicted = pred, Observed = test_data$Survived)   
data.frame(OOB_accuracy = oob_acc, Test_accuracy = test_acc)
```

Yes, Breiman was right because the OOB accuracy (70.3%) is relatively close to the test accuracy (76.5%). This is because Breiman believed that the OOB accuracy is the most unbiased estimator on the accuracy of the model when applied to the testing data. Since the OOB accuracy is roughly 6 percentage points away from the test accuracy, we can argue that Breiman was right about the nature of the OOB accuracy as an unbiased estimator. 

```{r}
# Question 4: Now fit an XGBoost model to do the same 
predictors <- c("Pclass", "Age", "Fare")
pclass_levels <- sort(unique(as.character(train_data$Pclass)))

# Build a numeric matrix
make_X <- function(d) {
  d <- as.data.frame(d)[, predictors]
  d$Pclass <- as.integer(factor(as.character(d$Pclass), levels = pclass_levels))
  as.matrix(d)
}

X_c <- make_X(train_data)
y_c <- as.numeric(as.character(train_data$Survived))   
X_t <- make_X(test_data)
y_t <- as.numeric(as.character(test_data$Survived))

dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(X_c, label = y_c)
dtest  <- xgb.DMatrix(X_t, label = y_t)
```

```{r}
# Tuning grid
learn_rate <- c(0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1)
reg_param  <- c(0.1, 1, 2, 5)
nmax       <- 1000                       # max number of boosted trees

tune   <- expand.grid(eta = learn_rate, lambda = reg_param)
curves <- matrix(NA, nrow = nmax, ncol = nrow(tune))   # CV error per round

for (i in seq_len(nrow(tune))) {
  params <- list(objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "error",
                 eta = tune$eta[i], lambda = tune$lambda[i],
                 max_depth = 3, subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8,
                 min_child_weight = 1, nthread = 2)
  cv <- xgb.cv(params, dtrain, nrounds = nmax, nfold = 5, verbose = 0)
  curves[, i] <- cv$evaluation_log$test_error_mean
}

tune$best_nrounds <- apply(curves, 2, which.min)
tune$cv_error     <- apply(curves, 2, min)
tune[order(tune$cv_error), ]              
```

```{r}
# CV error vs. number of trees - hold lambda constant 
sel <- which(tune$lambda == 1)
matplot(curves[, sel], type = "l", lty = 1, col = seq_along(sel), log = "x",
        xlab = "Number of boosted trees (log scale)", ylab = "5-fold CV error",
        main = "CV error vs. trees, by eta (lambda = 1)")
legend("topright", paste("eta =", tune$eta[sel]), col = seq_along(sel),
       lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

```{r}
# CV error vs. number of trees - one line per lambda (at the best eta)
best     <- tune[which.min(tune$cv_error), ]
sel      <- which(tune$eta == best$eta)
matplot(curves[, sel], type = "l", lty = 1, col = seq_along(sel), log = "x",
        xlab = "Number of boosted trees (log scale)", ylab = "5-fold CV error",
        main = paste0("CV error vs. trees, by lambda (eta = ", best$eta, ")"))
legend("topleft", paste("lambda =", tune$lambda[sel]), col = seq_along(sel),
       lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

```{r}
# Best CV error for every eta x lambda combination
err_mat <- tapply(tune$cv_error, list(tune$eta, tune$lambda), identity)
matplot(learn_rate, err_mat, type = "b", pch = 19, lty = 1,
        col = seq_along(reg_param),
        xlab = "eta (learning rate)", ylab = "Minimum CV error",
        main = "Minimum CV error by eta and lambda")
legend("bottomright", paste("lambda =", reg_param), col = seq_along(reg_param),
       pch = 19, bty = "n")
```

```{r}
# Final model and accuracy 
params_best <- list(objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "error",
                    eta = best$eta, lambda = best$lambda,
                    max_depth = 3, subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8,
                    min_child_weight = 1, nthread = 2)
bst <- xgb.train(params_best, dtrain, nrounds = best$best_nrounds)

prob <- predict(bst, dtest)
pred <- as.integer(prob > 0.5)

cm <- table(Predicted = pred, Observed = y_t)
cm
mosaicplot(cm, color = c("grey80", "steelblue"),
           main = "XGBoost confusion matrix (validation data)")

data.frame(CV_accuracy   = 1 - best$cv_error,
           Test_accuracy = mean(pred == y_t))
```
